title: PyTorch Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the PyTorch lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Create a tensor
entries.summary: A PyTorch tensor stores numbers with a shape and a data type. torch.tensor makes one from a small Python list.
notes: A tensor is a data container, not a trained model by itself.

entries.name: Inspect shape and dimensions
entries.summary: Shape gives the size of each dimension. ndim tells you how many dimensions there are.

example.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(tuple(x.shape), x.ndim)

notes: Two dimensions do not mean only two total values.

entries.name: Set a dtype
entries.summary: A dtype specifies how numbers are represented. Floating-point tensors are commonly used for model calculations and gradients.

example.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([1, 2], dtype=torch.float32)
print(x.dtype)

notes: Integer tensors cannot be used for every gradient calculation.

entries.name: Add matching values
entries.summary: Tensor arithmetic can combine matching positions. Shapes must match or follow broadcasting rules.

example.code:
import torch

a = torch.tensor([1, 2])
b = torch.tensor([3, 4])
print((a + b).tolist())

notes: Adding tensors is different from joining two Python lists.

entries.name: Use matrix multiplication
entries.summary: Matrix multiplication combines rows with columns. The inner dimensions must match. It is different from element-wise multiplication.

example.code:
import torch

a = torch.tensor([[1., 2.]])
b = torch.tensor([[3.], [4.]])
print((a @ b).item())

notes: Use * for element-wise multiplication and @ for matrix multiplication.

entries.name: Reshape values
entries.summary: reshape changes the layout of a tensor while keeping the same number of values.
notes: A new shape must contain the same total number of values.

entries.name: Track a gradient
entries.summary: requires_grad asks PyTorch to track operations for automatic differentiation. backward fills the gradient of the scalar result with respect to the input.

example.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
y = x * x
y.backward()
print(x.grad.item())

notes: Gradients accumulate by default; clear them between training steps.

entries.name: Disable tracking for a calculation
entries.summary: torch.no_grad runs operations without building a gradient-tracking graph. This is useful when you only need predictions.

example.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
with torch.no_grad():
    y = x * 2
print(y.requires_grad)

notes: no_grad and model.eval do different jobs; one does not replace the other.

entries.name: A linear layer learns weights
entries.summary: nn.Linear combines input features into output values using learned weights and a bias. Two inputs can produce one output.

example.code:
import torch

layer = torch.nn.Linear(2, 1)
x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0]])
print(tuple(layer(x).shape))

notes: Running an untrained layer does not make its predictions meaningful.

entries.name: Build a small sequential model
entries.summary: A sequential model applies layers in order. An activation such as ReLU keeps positive values and changes negative values to zero.

example.code:
import torch

model = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(2, 3), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(3, 1))
print(tuple(model(torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0]])).shape))

notes: Adjacent layers must have compatible sizes.

entries.name: One training step
entries.summary: A training step clears old gradients, computes loss, finds new gradients and updates weights. Each step has a separate job.

example.code:
import torch

model = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
x = torch.tensor([[1.], [2.]])
y = torch.tensor([[2.], [4.]])
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss = torch.nn.functional.mse_loss(model(x), y)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
print(loss.item() >= 0)

notes: Forgetting zero_grad can mix gradients from multiple steps unintentionally.

entries.name: Evaluation mode and checking
entries.summary: model.eval switches training-sensitive layers to evaluation behaviour. Use it with no_grad when making ordinary evaluation predictions.

example.code:
import torch

model = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(1, 1))
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    result = model(torch.tensor([[3.0]]))
print(tuple(result.shape))

notes: eval does not train a model and does not by itself disable gradients.
